In the Common shrew (Sorex araneus), neonates emerge after a brief gestation period of 21 days [tg = 21 days] when maintained at the species' typical body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. These altricial newborns weigh a mere 0.44 grams [Wwb = 0.44 grams] at birth, a remarkably low mass reflecting the highly altricial nature of soricid neonates, which are born blind, hairless, and entirely dependent on maternal care. This initial mass is less than six percent of the adult asymptotic wet weight of 8.4 grams [Wwi = 8.4 grams] that individuals ultimately reach, indicating the substantial growth trajectory that must be completed during the suckling and early juvenile stages. The period from parturition to nutritional independence is relatively compressed: weaning, defined as the cessation of lactation and the transition to solid food, occurs at 23 days after birth [tx = 23 days after birth] under the same thermal regime of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], at which point the young have achieved a wet weight at weaning of 7.6 grams [Wwx = 7.6 grams]. This rapid mass gain from the 0.44 gram neonate to the 7.6 gram weanling reflects intense maternal provisioning during the nursing period, a pattern consistent with the high metabolic demands of maintaining endothermy at such small body sizes.

Sexual maturation in Sorex araneus is achieved relatively late in life, especially when considered alongside its rapid postnatal development. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the production of viable gametes, is reached at 198 days after birth [tp = 198 days after birth] at 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This delay means that juveniles born early in the year typically mature only in the following spring, a pattern that synchronizes reproductive activity with favorable seasonal conditions. At the point of pubertal onset, individuals have attained a wet weight at puberty of approximately 8.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 8.2 grams], very close to the ultimate adult body mass of 8.4 grams [Wwi = 8.4 grams], suggesting that the completion of somatic growth and the onset of reproduction are tightly coupled in this species. This near-asymptotic mass at puberty is notable because it indicates that reproductive maturation occurs only after the majority of structural growth has been accomplished, a life-history strategy that prioritizes the attainment of adult body size before diverting resources into gamete production. The ultimate total length of adult Sorex araneus reaches 6 centimeters [Li = 6 centimeters], a modest dimension consistent with the extremely high mass-specific metabolic rates characteristic of shrews.

Under the thermal conditions typical of this species (38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]), the reproductive output of the Common shrew is constrained by its small body size. Females produce 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = 6 pups per litter], an intermediate litter size that balances the energetic costs of gestation and lactation against the need to produce sufficient offspring to offset high juvenile mortality rates. The frequency of such reproductive events is constrained by the short active season: females may produce approximately 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters per year], potentially yielding up to 18 offspring annually. This schedule is characteristic of soricids in seasonal environments where peak prey availability coincides with the breeding period.

Longevity in Sorex araneus is notably short compared to other small mammals of similar body mass, a pattern linked to its extraordinarily high metabolic rate. Life expectancy in the wild is heavily influenced by predation pressure and food availability, but the maximum recorded lifespan reaches approximately 1168 days [am = approximately 1168 days] in captive individuals maintained under optimal conditions at 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This compressed lifespan reflects the high costs of endothermy at such a small body size; shrews must consume up to twice their body weight in food daily merely to sustain resting metabolic demands, and the cumulative oxidative stress associated with such elevated metabolism likely accelerates senescence. In free-living populations, few individuals survive beyond their first breeding season, and mortality peaks sharply during winter when prey declines and thermoregulatory demands intensify.

The head-body length of Sorex araneus typically reaches 6 centimeters [Li = 6 centimeters] in fully grown adults, placing it among the smaller soricine shrews of the Palearctic. At 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], the gestation period of 21 days [tg = 21 days] is relatively short compared to other insectivores of comparable size, allowing females to compress their reproductive cycle within the limited window of favorable conditions. This rapid gestation is complemented by the similarly brief 23-day interval from birth to weaning (23 days after birth) [tx = 23 days after birth], resulting in a total generation time from conception to nutritional independence of only 44 days at a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. Such compressed developmental timelines are adaptive in environments where the growing season is short. The wet weight at birth of 0.44 grams [Wwb = 0.44 grams] underscores the extreme altriciality of this species, representing only about 5% of the adult asymptotic mass (8.4 grams) [Wwi = 8.4 grams] and necessitating intensive maternal investment during the nursing period.
